drill.title: Calibrate a thermometer in ice water
body: Every safe-temperature check this year depends on your thermometer reading correctly. A mixture of ice and water sits at 32°F, which makes it a reliable reference point.
The second part is a short knife-safety review. This unit's recipes call for diced onion and pepper, and the knife unit doesn't start until week 9.
steps: Fill a tall glass with ice, add cold water to just below the top of the ice, and stir. Let it stand 3 minutes.
Insert the probe at least 2 inches into the center of the glass, clear of the sides and bottom.
Wait for the reading to settle, about 30 seconds on a digital thermometer. It should read 32°F.

If it's more than 2°F off, recalibrate: most digital thermometers have a calibrate or reset function (see the manual); on a dial thermometer, an adult turns the nut under the dial with pliers until the needle reads 32°F. If it can't be adjusted, note the offset and correct for it every time.
Record readings for warm and cold tap water as well, so you get used to how quickly the probe settles.
Wash the probe in hot, soapy water. From now on, clean it after every use.
Knife review: set the cutting board on a damp paper towel so it can't slide. Grip the knife at the handle, and hold the food in a claw grip, fingertips curled under.
Halve an onion through the root, lay the halves flat side down, and chop them, moving your guide hand back with each cut. If the knife falls, step back and let it drop.
Use the onion in this week's recipe.

quiz.q: What should a calibrated thermometer read in ice water?
quiz.explain: An ice-water mixture stays at the freezing point of water, 32°F.

quiz.q: Why keep the probe away from the sides of the glass?
choices: The glass isn't the same temperature as the water
quiz.explain: You're measuring the water. The glass is warmer, so touching it skews the reading.

quiz.q: Your thermometer reads 35°F in ice water and can't be adjusted. A burger reads 162°F. What is it really?
quiz.explain: It reads 3°F high, so subtract 3. The burger needs another minute.

knowledge.title: Danger zone and how microorganisms grow
body: Most foodborne illness comes from microorganisms: bacteria such as Salmonella, E. coli, and Listeria, plus some viruses and parasites. They're common on raw meat, poultry, eggs, and produce, and you can't detect them by look, smell, or taste.

Bacteria multiply fastest between 40°F and 140°F, the range called the danger zone. Near body temperature, a population can double in as little as 20 minutes, so a few cells can become millions in a few hours.

Refrigeration (40°F or below) slows growth; freezing (0°F) stops it but doesn't kill anything. Cooking to a safe internal temperature kills most pathogens, and hot food held at 140°F or above stays out of the danger zone.

Some bacteria produce toxins that cooking doesn't break down, so reheating food that sat out too long doesn't make it safe. The USDA rule: cooked food goes into the fridge within 2 hours, or 1 hour when it's above 90°F.
steps: Leave your thermometer in a glass of water on the middle shelf of the fridge for an hour, then read it. Is the fridge at 40°F or below?
If you can, check the freezer the same way. Is it at 0°F or below?
If either runs warm, tell an adult. Turning the control a notch colder usually fixes it.

quiz.q: What is the danger zone?
quiz.explain: Bacteria multiply fastest in this range.

quiz.q: How long can cooked food stay at room temperature?
quiz.explain: After that, enough growth may have happened to make someone sick.

quiz.q: Why doesn't reheating rescue food that sat out all day?
choices: Some bacteria leave toxins that heat doesn't destroy
quiz.explain: Cooking kills the bacteria, but not every toxin they made.

sabbath.title: Label and date containers
body: Many families cook or prep ingredients ahead so they can spend the Sabbath resting instead of working in the kitchen. Food made ahead only helps if it's stored well, and this unit's Beyond the Recipe pages cover how: labeling, cooling, storing, and reheating.
Labels tell everyone what a container holds and when it was made, so nothing is eaten past its time or forgotten in the back.

The USDA guideline is 3 to 4 days in the fridge for cooked meat, poultry, soups, and stews. Many other leftovers keep longer, and hard-cooked eggs keep a week. Risk still climbs with time, because Listeria can grow at fridge temperatures and smell won't reveal it. Your family decides its own limits; the date on the label is what lets you apply them.
Frozen food stays safe indefinitely at 0°F, though it tastes best within 2 to 3 months.
steps: Put together a labeling kit: masking tape and a permanent marker, kept near the fridge.
Label every container from this week's cooking with the dish and the date it was cooked, for example "Shakshuka 10/4".
Go through the fridge with an adult and decide what's past your family's limit.
Move older food to the front so it gets used first.
Label anything you make ahead this week the moment it goes into the fridge.

quiz.q: What is the USDA guideline for cooked meat and poultry leftovers in the fridge?
quiz.explain: Other foods vary: many keep longer, and hard-cooked eggs keep a week.

quiz.q: Why can't you judge old leftovers by smell?
choices: The microorganisms that make food smell bad aren't the ones that make you sick
Smell only works on raw food
quiz.explain: Spoilage organisms cause smells and slime; pathogens like Listeria usually don't.

weeks.note: To 160°F

drill.title: Thick vs. thin: how size changes cooking time
body: Thickness changes cooking time more than most people expect, because heat has to travel from the surface to the center. Cook a thin piece and a thick piece side by side and track both with the thermometer.
A potato in the oven works as well as beef and costs far less. If you'd rather use beef, shape one of this week's burger patties thin and one thick when you make the recipe.
steps: Heat the oven to 400°F and line a sheet pan with foil.
Scrub a russet potato. Cut one slice about ¼ inch thick and one chunk about 1 inch thick. Rub both with a little oil and set them on the pan.
Bake them, and start a timer.
Every 5 minutes, pull the pan out with oven mitts and check the center of each piece with the thermometer. Record the time and temperature for both.
A potato is cooked through at about 205°F, when a fork slides in easily. Take each piece out when it gets there, and note its total time.
Compare: how much longer did the thick piece take? Did the outside look done before the center was?

With beef instead: cook a ¼-inch and a ¾-inch patty in a skillet over medium-high, check each from the side every minute after the flip, and pull each at 160°F. Wash your hands and the tongs after handling the raw beef.

quiz.q: A ¼-inch slice and a 1-inch chunk go in the oven together. Which reaches the target temperature first?
quiz.explain: Heat has a shorter path to the center of a thin piece.

quiz.q: A burger is brown all the way through. Is it done?
choices: Yes, if the juices run clear
quiz.explain: Ground beef can brown before it reaches a safe temperature, and can stay pink after it does. Color isn't reliable.

knowledge.title: Safe internal temperatures chart
body: The USDA publishes a minimum safe internal temperature for each kind of food, measured in the thickest part.

Poultry, whole or ground: 165°F. Ground beef and ground lamb: 160°F. Egg dishes: 160°F. Fish: 145°F. Leftovers and reheated food: 165°F. Whole cuts of beef and lamb (steaks, chops, roasts): 145°F with a 3-minute rest, which is medium.

Plenty of people eat steak rare (about 125°F) or medium-rare (about 135°F). For an intact whole cut, that's a much smaller risk than undercooking ground meat. Pathogens sit on the surface of a whole muscle, and a hard sear kills them, while the interior is close to sterile. Grinding spreads surface bacteria through the whole batch, which is why ground meat has to reach 160°F all the way through.

That reasoning only holds for intact cuts. It doesn't cover ground meat, poultry, or meat that has been needle-tenderized or injected with a marinade (the label will say so), and it doesn't cover anyone at higher risk: pregnant women, young children, older adults, or anyone with a weakened immune system.
For an accurate reading, put the tip in the thickest part, away from bone and the pan. With thin pieces, go in from the side, and check more than one piece.
steps: Make a temperature card: poultry 165°F, ground beef and lamb 160°F, eggs 160°F, fish 145°F, whole cuts 145°F (USDA), reheating 165°F.
Post it inside a cupboard door by the stove.

quiz.q: What temperature does ground turkey need to reach?
quiz.explain: All poultry, ground or whole, is 165°F.

quiz.q: Why is a rare steak lower risk than a rare burger?
choices: Grinding spreads surface bacteria through the meat; a steak's interior is nearly sterile
quiz.explain: Searing kills what's on a steak's surface. A burger's surface bacteria are mixed all the way through.

quiz.q: Which of these should never be served rare?
quiz.explain: Tenderizing pushes surface bacteria into the middle, so it needs the same care as ground meat.

sabbath.title: Cool a cooked dish in an ice bath
body: A large pot of hot food cools slowly, and its center can stay in the danger zone for hours, even in the fridge. It also warms everything stored around it.

The standard is two-stage cooling: from 140°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then to 40°F within 4 more. An ice bath handles the first stage; shallow containers, no more than 2 inches deep, handle the second.
steps: Pick something to cool: a pot of soup or rice, or a dish you're making ahead.
Fill the sink or a large bowl partway with ice and water.
Transfer the hot food to a metal bowl or pot and set it in the ice bath, with the water partway up the sides.
Stir every few minutes, and take the center temperature every 10 minutes. Record each reading.
At 70°F or below, divide it into shallow containers, cover, label, and refrigerate.
Note how long it took to go from 140°F to 70°F.

quiz.q: What is the time limit for cooling food from 140°F to 70°F?
quiz.explain: Then 4 more hours to reach 40°F.

quiz.q: Why do shallow containers cool faster than one deep one?
choices: The center is closer to the cold surface
quiz.explain: Less depth means heat has a shorter path out.

weeks.note: From the rice cooked and cooled in the drill

drill.title: Safe cooling of a batch of rice, saved for the fried rice
body: Cooked rice needs particular care. Raw rice often carries spores of Bacillus cereus, which survive cooking. If cooked rice sits warm, they grow and produce a toxin that reheating doesn't destroy. Cooled quickly and kept cold, rice is safe.
Do this the day before this week's fried rice. Fried rice works best with cold, day-old rice, so this batch goes straight into the recipe.
steps: Cook 2 cups of white rice in 3 cups of water: rinse, bring to a boil, then cover and cook on low until the water is absorbed.
Spread the hot rice in a thin layer on a sheet pan.
Let it cool uncovered until it stops steaming, about 20 minutes, then check the temperature in the middle of the layer.
Within 1 hour of cooking, and once it's below 70°F, pack it into a shallow container, cover, and label it.
Refrigerate it, and note the time from pot to fridge.
Use it in the fried rice within 1 to 2 days.

quiz.q: Why spread cooked rice on a sheet pan?
choices: A thin layer passes through the danger zone quickly
quiz.explain: More surface area means faster cooling.

quiz.q: Rice sat out warm all afternoon. What do you do?
quiz.explain: The Bacillus cereus toxin survives heat.

knowledge.title: Cross-contamination and board colors
body: Cross-contamination is the transfer of microorganisms from one food or surface to another, usually from raw meat to something that won't be cooked, by way of hands, knives, boards, or towels.

Commercial kitchens color-code cutting boards: red for raw meat, yellow for raw poultry, blue for raw fish, green for produce. At home, two boards cover it: one only for raw meat, poultry, and fish, and one for everything else.
With a single board, work from clean to raw: ready-to-eat foods and produce first, raw meat last, then wash the board, knife, and your hands in hot, soapy water.

Don't rinse raw poultry; it sprays bacteria around the sink and doesn't remove them. Cooked food goes on a clean plate, never the one that held it raw. Wash your hands after handling raw meat, eggs, or their packaging.
steps: Choose one cutting board for raw meat, poultry, and fish only, and mark it.
Go through this week's recipe and list every step that involves raw chicken or raw egg: what it touches, and where that gets washed.

quiz.q: With one cutting board, what order do you work in?
quiz.explain: Anything cut after raw meat on the same board picks up its bacteria.

quiz.q: Should you rinse raw chicken?
choices: No, it spreads bacteria without removing them
quiz.explain: Cooking to 165°F is what makes chicken safe.

quiz.q: The chicken is cooked. Where does it go?
choices: The plate it sat on raw
quiz.explain: Anything that held raw meat still carries its bacteria.

sabbath.title: Make a dish ahead and store it
body: This week puts the unit together: cook a dish ahead, cool it fast, and store it so it's safe and good when it's eaten. Many families do this before the Sabbath so they can rest; it works just as well for a busy weeknight.
Stored food stays out of the danger zone: cold at 40°F or below, or hot at 140°F or above if it's being held for a meal.
Braises like chicken adobo improve after a night in the fridge, which makes them good make-ahead choices.
steps: Pick a dish from this week to make ahead: the fried rice, chicken adobo, or something your family will eat later in the week.
Cook it a day or two before it's needed, and cool it quickly in shallow containers (week 2).
Cover and label it (week 1), and store it on a shelf, not in the door, which runs warmer.
Confirm the fridge is at 40°F or below.
If your family holds food hot for a meal, check that it stays at 140°F or above.

quiz.q: Where should make-ahead food be stored in the fridge?
quiz.explain: The door warms up every time it opens.

quiz.q: What temperature does hot-held food need to stay at?
quiz.explain: Below 140°F, it's in the danger zone.

weeks.note: Or beef kofta to 160°F, or turkey meatloaf to 165°F

drill.title: Set up a clean station unaided
body: Set up your own clean station without help. An adult checks it against the list but doesn't step in.
steps: Clear the counter of anything you won't use. Wash it with hot, soapy water and dry it.
Wash your hands with soap for at least 20 seconds.
Set out both cutting boards, raw-meat and general, each on a damp paper towel.
Set out a plate for raw meat, a separate plate for cooked food, and a bowl for scraps.
Calibrate the thermometer in ice water (week 1) and keep it within reach.
Fill one side of the sink or a dishpan with hot, soapy water for washing as you go.
Have the adult check your setup against this list, then cook this week's recipe from it.

quiz.q: How long should you wash your hands?
quiz.explain: That's the CDC guideline, with soap, scrubbing every surface.

quiz.q: Why two plates?
choices: One for raw meat, one for cooked food
quiz.explain: Cooked food never goes back on the raw plate.

knowledge.title: Food safety quiz
body: This quiz covers the whole unit. Answer from memory, then review anything you missed in weeks 1 to 3.

quiz.q: What is the danger zone?
quiz.explain: Bacteria multiply fastest in this range.

quiz.q: What temperature does chicken need to reach?
quiz.explain: All poultry, whole or ground.

quiz.q: What temperature does ground beef need to reach?
quiz.explain: Ground beef and ground lamb are 160°F.

quiz.q: Why can a steak be eaten rare when a burger can't?
choices: A steak's bacteria are on the surface, which the sear kills
quiz.explain: Grinding mixes surface bacteria through the whole patty.

quiz.q: What does a calibrated thermometer read in ice water?
quiz.explain: That's the reference point for checking it.

quiz.q: How long can cooked food sit out before refrigerating?
quiz.explain: After that, throw it out.

quiz.q: How do you cool a pot of soup quickly?
choices: Ice bath, stirring, then shallow containers
Put the whole pot in the fridge
Leave it on the stove overnight
quiz.explain: 140°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then 40°F within 4 more.

quiz.q: With one cutting board, what goes last?
quiz.explain: Then the board gets washed.

quiz.q: How hot should reheated leftovers get?
quiz.explain: Measured in the center.

quiz.q: What is the USDA guideline for cooked meat and poultry leftovers in the fridge?
quiz.explain: Many other leftovers keep longer, but risk still rises with time, because Listeria grows even in the fridge.

quiz.q: Rice sat out warm all afternoon. What do you do?
quiz.explain: Bacillus cereus toxin survives reheating.

sabbath.title: Reheat a stored dish to 165°F
body: Reheated leftovers need to reach 165°F at the center of the thickest piece. Warm to the touch isn't the same thing.
Reheat only what you'll eat. Each round of reheating and cooling costs quality and adds time in the danger zone.
steps: Choose a stored dish: this week's meatloaf, or something you made ahead.
Oven: portions in a baking dish with a splash of water or broth, covered with foil, at 350°F. Microwave: cover loosely, and stir or rotate every minute or two.
Check the center of the thickest piece. Keep heating until it reads 165°F.
Note the method and how long it took.
Serve it, or put it back in the fridge within 2 hours. Don't reheat the same portion twice.

quiz.q: Where do you check the temperature of reheated food?
choices: The center of the thickest piece
quiz.explain: The center heats last.

quiz.q: Why stir or rotate food in the microwave?
choices: Microwaves heat unevenly and leave cold spots
quiz.explain: A cold spot can still be in the danger zone.

drill.title: Bloom yeast; test water temperature
body: You'll test yeast in water at three temperatures, side by side, and see for yourself why the recipe asks for 105 to 110°F. Use the thermometer you calibrated in week 1.
steps: Set out 3 clear glasses or jars and label them: cool, warm, hot.

Fill each with ½ cup of water: about 80°F in the first, 105 to 110°F in the second, and 140°F in the third. Warm the water in the microwave and check each glass with the thermometer, adjusting with hot or cold water until it reads right.
Stir ½ teaspoon of sugar into each glass.
Sprinkle ½ teaspoon of active dry yeast over each, and start a 10-minute timer.
At 5 minutes and at 10 minutes, look at each glass. Note how much foam there is and how it smells.
Write down what you saw: which bloomed fastest, which bloomed slowly, and which didn't bloom at all.
Pour the glasses down the drain and rinse them.

quiz.q: Which glass should show no foam?
quiz.explain: Water that hot kills yeast.

quiz.q: The 80°F glass foamed, but slowly. Why?
choices: Cool water slows yeast but doesn't kill it
quiz.explain: Yeast still works when it's cool, just more slowly.

knowledge.title: How yeast makes dough rise
body: Baker's yeast is a single-celled fungus, Saccharomyces cerevisiae. A packet holds billions of them, dried and dormant. Warm water wakes them up.

Once awake, yeast feeds on sugars in the dough, some added and some released from the flour's starch by its own enzymes. It breaks them down by fermentation and gives off two things: carbon dioxide gas and a little alcohol (ethanol).

The gas is what raises bread. Kneading builds gluten, a stretchy network that traps the gas in thousands of tiny bubbles, so the dough swells instead of letting it escape. In the oven, the gas expands, the alcohol bakes off, and the heat kills the yeast at about 140°F. The bubbles set in place as the crumb.

Temperature runs the whole process. Yeast works best around 75 to 80°F in a rising dough. Cold slows it down; that's why a dough can rise overnight in the fridge. Water above about 130°F starts to kill it, which is why you check the water before the yeast goes in.
Fermentation also makes flavor. A dough that rises slowly, in a cool kitchen or the fridge, tastes fuller than one rushed in a warm spot.

quiz.q: What is baker's yeast?
quiz.explain: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a living fungus, dried and dormant in the packet.

quiz.q: Which gas raises bread dough?
quiz.explain: Yeast gives it off as it ferments sugar. Steam helps in the oven, as in pita.

quiz.q: What traps the gas in the dough?
quiz.explain: Gluten's stretchy network holds the gas in tiny bubbles.

quiz.q: What happens to yeast in the oven?
choices: It keeps working until the bread cools
quiz.explain: By then it has done its work, and the bubbles set as the crumb.

quiz.q: Why can dough rise overnight in the fridge?
choices: Cold slows yeast down without killing it
quiz.explain: That slow rise also gives the bread more flavor.

sabbath.title: Bake and freeze pita
body: Bread freezes better than almost anything you'll cook. Frozen within a few hours of baking, it tastes nearly fresh when it's reheated. Left on the counter, it goes stale in a day or two, and a stale pita cracks instead of folding.

Staling isn't drying out. The starch in bread slowly recrystallizes as it cools, and that's what makes it firm. The fridge speeds that up, so bread keeps worse there than on the counter. The freezer stops it.
Many families bake ahead like this so there's bread on hand for busy days, or so they can focus on resting.
steps: Set aside some of this week's pitas, or bake a second batch.
Let them cool completely, about 30 minutes, in their towel. Warm pitas sweat in a bag, and the drops of water turn to ice.
Stack them with a square of parchment between each, so you can take out one at a time.
Slide the stack into a freezer bag, press out the air, and seal it. Label it with what it is and the date.
Freeze for up to 3 months.
To serve, wrap the frozen pitas in foil and heat them at 350°F for 10 to 15 minutes, or thaw one on the counter for 15 minutes and warm it in a dry skillet for 30 seconds a side.

quiz.q: Why not keep bread in the fridge?
choices: The cold makes it go stale faster
quiz.explain: Cold speeds up the starch recrystallizing. The freezer stops it.

quiz.q: Why cool the pitas before bagging them?
choices: Warm bread sweats, and the water turns to ice
quiz.explain: Ice crystals make the bread soggy when it thaws.

drill.title: Knead and windowpane test
body: You'll knead a small dough by hand and test it as you go, so you learn what a developed dough feels like. There's no yeast in it; the drill is about gluten.
steps: Stir together 1 cup of all-purpose flour, ⅓ cup of water, and a pinch of salt in a bowl until it forms a rough dough.
Turn it out and knead: push it away with the heel of your hand, fold it back, turn it a quarter turn, and repeat in a steady rhythm.
After 2 minutes, pinch off a grape-sized piece and try the windowpane test: stretch it slowly between your fingers and thumbs into a thin sheet. Note where it tears.
Knead 3 more minutes and test again. Then 3 more, and test again.
Note how the dough changed: how sticky it is, how smooth, and how far it stretched each time.
When a piece stretches thin enough to see light through, the dough is developed. Note how many minutes it took.
Roll the dough thin and cook it in a dry skillet like Unleavened flatbread, or throw it out.

quiz.q: The test piece tore before it went thin. What next?
choices: Knead a few more minutes and test again
quiz.explain: The gluten isn't developed yet.

quiz.q: How does dough change as you knead it?
quiz.explain: The gluten network is organizing.

knowledge.title: Gluten and kneading
body: Wheat flour holds two proteins, glutenin and gliadin. Dry, they do nothing. When water is added, they link up into gluten. Glutenin makes it springy and strong, and gliadin makes it stretchy.

Kneading lines those links up. At first the dough is shaggy and tears easily. As you push, fold, and turn it, the strands lengthen and organize into a network that stretches without breaking. That's what the windowpane test shows.
A strong network matters most for a tall loaf. It has to hold its gas through a long rise and half an hour in the oven. A flatbread, baked in minutes, needs less.

Other ingredients change gluten. Fat (butter, oil, egg yolk) coats the strands so the crumb is soft and tender; that's an enriched dough. Salt tightens the network and slows the yeast a little. Bread flour has more protein than all-purpose, so it builds stronger gluten and a chewier bread.

Gluten is also why some people can't eat bread. In people with celiac disease, gluten triggers an immune reaction that damages the small intestine. Gluten-free breads use other starches and binders, and they behave differently in every step you're learning.

quiz.q: Which two proteins form gluten?
quiz.explain: Water lets them link; kneading lines them up.

quiz.q: What does kneading do?
choices: Lines up gluten strands into a strong network
quiz.explain: That network traps the yeast's gas.

quiz.q: Why is an enriched dough softer?
quiz.explain: Butter, oil, and egg yolk tenderize the crumb.

quiz.q: Why would a baker pick bread flour?
choices: Its higher protein builds stronger gluten
quiz.explain: Stronger gluten makes a taller, chewier loaf.

sabbath.title: Bread in the Bible: daily bread and the bread of life (Matthew 6:11; John 6:35)
body: Bread comes up more than almost any other food in the Bible. It stands for the food a person needs to live, and often for more than that.

In the wilderness, God fed Israel with manna, "bread from heaven" (Exodus 16:4). Each morning the people gathered what they needed for that day. Manna kept overnight spoiled, except the double portion gathered on the sixth day, which kept (Exodus 16:16–24). It taught them to depend on God one day at a time.
Jesus taught his disciples to pray, "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matthew 6:11). The prayer asks for what's needed today, not a store for years.

After feeding five thousand people with five loaves (John 6:1–14), Jesus told the crowd, who had brought up the manna, "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger" (John 6:35). Bread keeps a body alive for a day; he spoke of himself as what keeps a person alive for good.
steps: Read Exodus 16:4–5 and 16:13–24.
Read Matthew 6:9–13.
Read John 6:26–35.
Answer in writing: what did gathering manna each morning teach Israel?
Answer in writing: why do you think Jesus compared himself to bread, and not to some other food?
Share your answers with an adult at a meal this week, with a slice of this week's loaf.

quiz.q: What did Israel gather each morning in the wilderness?
quiz.explain: "Bread from heaven" (Exodus 16:4).

quiz.q: Where is "Give us this day our daily bread"?
quiz.explain: It's part of the prayer Jesus taught in Matthew 6.

quiz.q: What happened just before Jesus said "I am the bread of life"?
choices: He fed five thousand people with five loaves
quiz.explain: The crowd followed him after the feeding (John 6:1–14, 26).

drill.title: Shape even rolls by weight
body: Bakeries weigh dough because eyes are poor judges of size. You'll divide a practice dough by weight and shape tight, even balls.
steps: Stir together 1½ cups of all-purpose flour, ½ cup of water, and a pinch of salt until it forms a dough. Knead it until it's smooth, about 3 minutes.
Before using the scale, cut the dough by eye into 8 pieces you think are equal. Weigh each one and write the weights down.
Press the pieces back together. Weigh the whole dough and divide by 8. That's your target.
Cut 8 pieces again, this time weighing each. Pinch dough from heavy pieces onto light ones until each is within 3 grams of the target.
Shape each piece into a ball: cup it under your palm on a bare spot of counter and roll it in small circles until the top is smooth and tight.
Compare your two sets of weights. How far off were your eyes?
Roll the balls flat and cook them in a dry skillet like Unleavened flatbread, or throw them out.

quiz.q: Why weigh dough instead of cutting it by eye?
choices: So every roll bakes through at the same time
quiz.explain: Small rolls overbake while large ones stay doughy.

quiz.q: Why shape on a bare spot of counter, not on flour?
choices: A little stickiness gives the dough grip to tighten
quiz.explain: On flour, the ball just slides and never builds a tight skin.

knowledge.title: Proofing: under vs. over
body: Proofing is the last rise, after shaping. It decides how a bread turns out more than any other step, and there's no clock for it. You judge it by the dough.

The poke test: flour a fingertip and press it about ½ inch into the side of the dough. If the dent springs back right away, the dough is underproofed. If it springs back slowly and leaves a small dent, it's ready. If it doesn't spring back at all, or the dough sighs and sinks, it's overproofed.
Underproofed bread is dense and tight. It rises hard in the oven and often bursts open along a side, because the yeast still has a lot of gas to give and the gluten is still tight.

Overproofed bread rises too far before baking. The gluten stretches thin and weak, the yeast runs out of sugar, and the loaf collapses or spreads flat in the oven, with big holes under the crust and a sour, boozy smell.

Temperature sets the pace. A warm kitchen (80°F) might proof rolls in 30 minutes; a cool one (68°F) might take an hour and a half. The fridge (below 40°F) slows it to overnight, which is called a cold proof or retarding the dough. That's the make-ahead method in this week's Beyond the Recipe.

quiz.q: You poke the dough and the dent springs right back. What does that mean?
choices: It's underproofed; give it more time
quiz.explain: Ready dough springs back slowly and leaves a small dent.

quiz.q: What does overproofed bread do in the oven?
quiz.explain: The gluten is stretched weak, and the yeast has run out of food.

quiz.q: Why might rolls proof faster on one day than another?
quiz.explain: Yeast works faster when it's warm.

quiz.q: What does a cold proof in the fridge do?
choices: Slows the yeast so dough can wait overnight
quiz.explain: It's also called retarding the dough.

sabbath.title: Shape rolls a day ahead; cold proof overnight
body: A cold proof splits rolls across two days. You do the mixing and shaping one day, and the next day you only bake them. The long, cool rise also gives them more flavor.

The fridge keeps a dough with milk and egg safe, because it stays below 40°F, out of the danger zone. Shaped dough keeps there for 8 to 16 hours. Past about a day, the yeast runs out of food and the rolls overproof.
Many families do the shaping a day ahead so baking day is short, or so they can focus on resting.
steps: Make this week's roll dough and let it rise once, as the recipe says.
Weigh, divide, and shape the rolls into the buttered dish.
Cover the dish tightly with plastic wrap or a lid, and put it straight in the fridge. Label it with the time.
Leave it 8 to 16 hours.

The next day, take the dish out and leave it on the counter, still covered, until the rolls are puffy and touching and pass the poke test. This usually takes 1 to 2 hours, because the dough starts cold.
Heat the oven to 375°F and bake them as the recipe says, to 190°F in the middle roll.
Note how the cold-proofed rolls compare with ones made the same day: flavor, rise, and color.

quiz.q: Why is dough with milk and egg safe overnight in the fridge?
choices: It stays below 40°F, out of the danger zone
quiz.explain: Refrigerator temperatures keep it out of the 40–140°F range.

quiz.q: Why do cold rolls need 1 to 2 hours on the counter?
choices: The dough has to warm up and finish proofing
So they don't crack the dish
quiz.explain: Yeast is slow when cold. Use the poke test, not the clock.

weeks.note: Shape 2 or 3 as small braids or knots

drill.title: Braid a dough
body: A three-strand braid is the classic challah shape. You'll practice it with a plain dough until it's smooth and even, before you braid this week's challah on your own.
steps: Stir together 1½ cups of all-purpose flour, ½ cup of water, and a pinch of salt. Knead it until it's smooth, about 3 minutes, and cut it into 3 pieces of the same weight.
Roll each piece into a rope about 12 inches long, a little thicker in the middle than at the ends. If a rope shrinks back, let it rest 5 minutes.
Lay the ropes side by side, running away from you, and pinch them together at the far end.
Braid: cross the right rope over the middle one, then the left rope over the new middle one. Keep going, right over middle, left over middle, snug but not stretched.
At the end, pinch the three ropes together and tuck both pinched ends under the loaf.
Unbraid it, roll the ropes again, and braid a second time, this time starting from the middle and working to each end, turning the loaf around between halves. Compare the two: which is more even?
If you have time, try a four-strand or a round braid from a video or book, and note the pattern you used.
Roll the dough out and cook it in a dry skillet like Unleavened flatbread, or throw it out.

quiz.q: In a three-strand braid, where does each outside rope go?
quiz.explain: Right over middle, then left over middle.

quiz.q: Why braid from the middle out to each end?
choices: The loaf comes out even, thick in the middle and tapered
quiz.explain: Braiding end to end tends to leave one end fat and one thin.

knowledge.title: Doneness: color, sound, 190°F inside
body: This week you judge doneness three ways, then take the unit quiz.

Color: the crust browns through the Maillard reaction, where proteins and sugars react above about 300°F. An egg wash, honey, or milk adds proteins and sugars, so enriched breads brown sooner and darker. That's why color alone can fool you.

Sound: tip a loaf over (with oven mitts) and tap the bottom. A done loaf sounds hollow, because the crumb has set and dried. A dull thud means it's still wet inside. It's a useful check, but hard to read on a soft, rich loaf.

Temperature: the thermometer is the sure test. Enriched breads like sandwich loaves, rolls, and challah are done at 190°F in the center. Lean breads (flour, water, yeast, salt) go to about 200 to 210°F for a crisp crust and an open crumb. At these temperatures, the starch has absorbed water and set; this is called gelatinization.
Underbaked bread is gummy and dense in the middle and may sink as it cools. Bread keeps cooking for a while after it comes out, so it's cooled before slicing.

quiz.q: What temperature is an enriched bread done at?
quiz.explain: Lean breads go higher, to about 200 to 210°F.

quiz.q: Why does an egg-washed loaf brown early?
choices: Egg adds proteins and sugars for the Maillard reaction
quiz.explain: That's why color isn't enough.

quiz.q: What does a hollow sound tell you?
choices: The crumb has set and dried
quiz.explain: A dull thud means it's still wet.

quiz.q: Unit review: what water temperature wakes active dry yeast?
quiz.explain: Above about 130°F starts to kill it.

quiz.q: Unit review: which gas raises yeast dough?
quiz.explain: Yeast gives it off as it ferments sugar.

quiz.q: Unit review: what does the windowpane test show?
quiz.explain: The dough stretches thin enough to see light through.

quiz.q: Unit review: a gentle poke springs back slowly and leaves a small dent. The dough is…
quiz.explain: Fast spring-back is under; none at all is over.

quiz.q: Unit review: why is bread kept in the freezer, not the fridge?
choices: The fridge speeds staling; the freezer stops it
The fridge is unsafe for bread
Bread can't be frozen after baking
quiz.explain: Staling is starch recrystallizing, fastest just above freezing.

quiz.q: Unit review: why weigh dough when dividing it?
quiz.explain: Sizes by eye can differ by a third.

sabbath.title: Leaven and unleavened bread (Exodus 12:15–20; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8)
body: Leaven is anything that makes dough rise by fermentation: yeast, or a sourdough starter, a piece of old dough kept back to start the next batch. You've baked with it for four weeks. Scripture uses it in two ways, as a real food and as a picture.

As a food: at the first Passover, Israel left Egypt in such a hurry that their dough had no time to rise (Exodus 12:34, 39). God commanded them to eat unleavened bread for seven days each year, from the evening of the 14th day of the first month to the evening of the 21st, and to put all leaven out of their houses (Exodus 12:15–20). Deuteronomy calls it "the bread of affliction," eaten to remember leaving Egypt in haste (Deuteronomy 16:3).

As a picture: Paul writes, "a little leaven leavens the whole lump" (1 Corinthians 5:6). A pinch of starter works through an entire batch of dough. He uses that to show how one wrong left alone spreads through a whole community, and tells the believers to "celebrate the festival … with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" (1 Corinthians 5:8).

Leaven isn't always bad in Scripture. The two loaves offered at the Feast of Weeks were baked with leaven (Leviticus 23:17), and Jesus compared the kingdom of heaven to leaven that a woman worked into three measures of flour until all of it rose (Matthew 13:33).
Families keep these days in different ways. This app shows the unleavened days a family sets and plans around leavened recipes on those days.
steps: Read Exodus 12:14–20 and 12:33–39.
Read 1 Corinthians 5:6–8.
Read Leviticus 23:15–17 and Matthew 13:33.
From your own baking, explain in writing how "a little leaven leavens the whole lump" works in a bowl of dough. How much yeast went into your challah, and how much dough did it raise?
Answer in writing: in 1 Corinthians 5, what does leaven stand for, and what does unleavened bread stand for?
Share your answers with an adult over this week's challah.

quiz.q: Why was Israel's bread unleavened when they left Egypt?
choices: They left in haste, before the dough could rise
quiz.explain: Exodus 12:34 and 39.

quiz.q: How many days is unleavened bread eaten in Exodus 12?
quiz.explain: Exodus 12:15.

quiz.q: What does Paul use leaven to picture in 1 Corinthians 5?
choices: Wrong that spreads through a whole community
quiz.explain: "A little leaven leavens the whole lump" (1 Corinthians 5:6).

quiz.q: Which offering was baked with leaven?
choices: The two loaves at the Feast of Weeks
quiz.explain: Leviticus 23:17.

weeks.note: The pico de gallo is the knife work

drill.title: Claw grip; dice 3 onions
body: Dicing three onions in a row is how chefs learn the claw and the pinch grip until they're automatic. Go slowly; speed comes on its own. An adult is nearby the whole time.
steps: Set the cutting board on a damp paper towel. Hold the chef's knife in a pinch grip: thumb and bent pointer finger pinching the blade just in front of the handle.
Cut the first onion in half through the root, peel it, and lay one half flat side down.
Hold it with the claw: fingertips curled under, knuckles forward, the flat of the blade against your knuckles. Cut strips ¼ inch apart toward the root, stopping just before it.
Cut across the strips, ¼ inch apart, moving your claw hand back a little after each cut.
Dice the other half, then the second and third onions the same way.
Spread a spoonful of each onion's dice on the board and compare: are the third onion's cubes more even than the first's?
Put the diced onion in a container, label it, and keep it for this week's tacos and Beyond the Recipe (it keeps 5 to 7 days in the fridge).

quiz.q: In the claw, where are your fingertips?
choices: Flat on top of the food
quiz.explain: The knuckles guide the blade; the fingertips stay back.

quiz.q: Why does a sharp knife make you cry less over onions?
choices: It crushes fewer cells, so less of the stinging gas is released
quiz.explain: Crushed onion cells release a gas that stings your eyes.

knowledge.title: Parts of a knife; knife types
body: A chef's knife has names for every part, and each part has a job. The tip does fine work, like the cuts toward an onion's root. The edge runs from tip to heel; its curved belly is what lets the blade rock. The heel, the back of the edge, is the strongest part, for hard things like carrots. The spine is the dull top edge, where your hand rests when you rock-chop. The bolster is the thick band where the blade meets the handle, and the tang is the part of the blade that runs into the handle. A full tang, running the whole length, makes a knife sturdy and balanced.

Most cooking needs three knives. A chef's knife (8 inches is the usual size) does nearly all the cutting. A paring knife, 3 to 4 inches, is for small work in the hand, like hulling a strawberry. A serrated bread knife saws through crust and tomato skin without crushing. A santoku is a Japanese chef's knife with a flatter edge, better for chopping straight down than rocking.

A sharp knife is safer than a dull one. A dull blade needs more force, skids off a tomato skin or an onion's curve, and slips toward your hand. Other rules: cut on a board that can't slide; carry a knife point down at your side; never try to catch a falling knife; and never leave one in a sink of soapy water, where someone will reach in without seeing it.

quiz.q: Which part of the knife does your other hand rest on when you rock-chop?
quiz.explain: The spine is the dull top of the blade.

quiz.q: Which part of the edge is best for a hard carrot?
quiz.explain: The heel is the strongest part of the edge.

quiz.q: Which knife cuts tomato skin and bread crust without crushing?
quiz.explain: Its teeth saw instead of pressing.

quiz.q: Why is a dull knife more dangerous than a sharp one?
choices: It needs more force and skids toward your hand
quiz.explain: A sharp blade bites where you aim it.

quiz.q: A knife falls off the counter. What do you do?
choices: Step back and let it fall
quiz.explain: Never try to catch a falling knife.

sabbath.title: Chop vegetables ahead and store them
body: Knife work is most of the time a meal takes, and much of it can be done days ahead. Many families chop ahead like this so busy evenings are quick, or so they can focus on resting.

Some vegetables keep well cut: onions, bell peppers, carrots, and celery last 3 to 5 days (onions up to a week) in a sealed container in the fridge. A folded paper towel in the container soaks up moisture that would make them slimy.
Others don't: cut tomatoes turn mealy, cut cucumbers go soft, and cut potatoes and apples turn brown. Potatoes can wait under cold water in the fridge for up to a day. Cut those on the day.
steps: Plan a meal for later in the week that uses onions, peppers, or carrots.
Dice, slice, or julienne what it needs, using this unit's cuts.
Line each container with a folded paper towel and pack each vegetable in its own container.
Label each one with what it is and the date, as in week 1.
Store them in the fridge, and use them within the times above.
When you cook the meal, note how much time the prep saved.

quiz.q: Which vegetable should you not cut days ahead?
quiz.explain: Cut tomatoes turn mealy and watery.

quiz.q: Why put a paper towel in the container?
choices: It soaks up moisture that makes vegetables slimy
quiz.explain: Damp vegetables spoil faster.

weeks.note: A fine mince

drill.title: Mince parsley and garlic
body: A mince is the finest cut, about the size of a grain of rice. You'll mince parsley, which is soft and slips, and garlic, which is small and sticky.
steps: Hone the knife, with an adult watching.
Wash a bunch of parsley and dry it completely in a kitchen towel. Pull off the leaves.
Gather the leaves into a tight pile. Rock the knife through it, tip on the board and your other hand flat on the spine. Gather the pile and rock through again until no whole leaves are left.
Peel a few garlic cloves: lay one under the flat of the blade, edge facing away from you, and press down with the heel of your hand until it cracks. The skin slips off.
Slice each clove thin, then rock through the slices until they're minced. Gather and repeat.
Compare your minced parsley with a grain of rice. Mince again anything much bigger.
Use the parsley in this week's tabbouleh and the garlic in a meal this week. Store the garlic in the fridge, covered, and use it within a day or two.

quiz.q: When you crush a garlic clove with the flat of the knife, where does the edge face?
quiz.explain: The heel of your hand presses the flat, far from the edge.

quiz.q: Why should garlic in oil never sit at room temperature?
choices: It can grow Clostridium botulinum, whose toxin is deadly
quiz.explain: Garlic can carry the spores, and oil shuts out air, which they need. Keep it in the fridge, briefly, or frozen.

knowledge.title: Honing vs. sharpening
body: Under a microscope, a knife's edge is a thin ridge of metal. As you cut, it bends over to one side, a little at a time, like the tip of a page that's been folded. The knife feels dull even though the metal is still there.
Honing fixes that. A honing steel (a rod with a handle) pushes the bent edge back into line. It removes almost no metal, so you can hone every time you cook. Chefs hone before each use.

Sharpening is different: it grinds away metal to make a brand-new edge. It's done with a whetstone, a sharpener, or by a professional, every few months for a home cook. Honing can't fix an edge that's worn away; sharpening can.
How to tell: a honed, sharp knife slides into a tomato's skin with no pressure. If it skids even after honing, it needs sharpening.

To hone, an adult shows you first. Stand the steel straight up with its tip on a folded towel. Hold the blade against it at a slight angle, about 15 degrees, heel at the top. Draw the blade down and toward you so the whole edge, heel to tip, touches the steel. Do the other side the same way, and repeat 5 or 6 times on each side. Light pressure; it isn't a sword fight.

quiz.q: What does honing do?
choices: Pushes a bent edge back into line
quiz.explain: It removes almost no metal.

quiz.q: How often can you hone?
quiz.explain: Chefs hone before each use.

quiz.q: A freshly honed knife still skids on a tomato. What does it need?
quiz.explain: The edge is worn away and has to be ground new.

quiz.q: Where does the steel's tip rest when you hone?
choices: On a folded towel on the counter
quiz.explain: Standing it up keeps the blade moving down, away from you.

sabbath.title: Store prepped herbs so they stay fresh
body: Fresh herbs wilt fast, but stored the right way, most keep a week or more.

Tender herbs (parsley, cilantro, mint, dill) keep like cut flowers: trim the stems, stand them in a jar with an inch of water, cover the tops loosely with a bag, and keep them in the fridge. Basil is the exception; it keeps on the counter, because cold turns its leaves black.
Woody herbs (thyme, rosemary, oregano) keep wrapped in a barely damp paper towel in a bag in the fridge.

Chopped herbs last a day or two in a container lined with a paper towel. To keep them longer, freeze them: pack chopped herbs into an ice cube tray, cover with water or olive oil, and freeze. A cube drops straight into a soup or sauce. Many families keep herbs ready like this so cooking ahead is quick, or so they can focus on resting.
steps: Set up a jar of parsley or cilantro: trim the stems, stand them in an inch of water, and cover loosely with a bag. Put it in the fridge.
Wrap any woody herbs in a barely damp paper towel and seal them in a bag.
Chop a handful of herbs and freeze them in an ice cube tray, covered with water or oil. When frozen, move the cubes to a labeled bag.
Change the jar's water every 2 or 3 days.
Check the herbs after a week, and note which method kept them best.

quiz.q: How do you store parsley so it stays fresh longest?
choices: Stems in a jar of water in the fridge, loosely covered
On the counter in the sun
quiz.explain: Like cut flowers.

quiz.q: Why does basil stay out of the fridge?
quiz.explain: Basil is damaged by cold.

weeks.note: Julienne

drill.title: Julienne carrots and peppers
body: A julienne is a matchstick about ⅛ inch thick and 2 to 3 inches long. You'll julienne carrots and peppers, then measure your work.
steps: Peel 2 carrots and cut them into 3-inch pieces.
Slice a thin strip off one side of each piece and lay it on that flat side. Slice it the long way into planks ⅛ inch thick.
Stack 2 or 3 planks, hold them with the claw, and slice them the long way into ⅛-inch matchsticks.
Cut the top and bottom off a bell pepper, open it flat, cut away the ribs, and julienne it skin side down.
Line up 10 carrot matchsticks against a ruler. How many are within ⅛ inch of each other?
Store the matchsticks in a container in the fridge (carrots in a little cold water) and use them in this week's stir-fry or as a snack within 3 days.

quiz.q: How big is a julienne?
choices: About ⅛ inch thick and 2 to 3 inches long
quiz.explain: A thin matchstick.

quiz.q: Why do you cut the pepper skin side down?
choices: The knife skids on the shiny skin
quiz.explain: Flesh side up, the blade bites right away.

knowledge.title: Why even cuts cook evenly
body: Heat moves into food from the outside in, by conduction. The outside of a piece gets hot first, and the middle is the last part to reach the temperature you want.

Thickness matters more than you'd guess. The time for heat to reach the center grows with the square of the thickness: a piece twice as thick takes about four times as long to cook through. That's why a ¼-inch matchstick and a ½-inch one, side by side in a pan, can't finish together.

Size also changes surface area. Small pieces have more surface for their size, so they brown faster, take up more sauce, and lose water faster. Even cuts brown evenly; mixed sizes give you burnt crumbs and raw chunks in the same bite.

Fast methods, like stir-frying and sautéing, are the least forgiving: there are only a few minutes for heat to reach every piece. Slow methods, like a stew, give big pieces time to catch up. So the faster the cooking, the more even the cuts need to be.

quiz.q: A carrot stick is twice as thick as another. About how much longer does it take to cook through?
quiz.explain: Time grows with the square of the thickness.

quiz.q: How does heat get to the middle of a piece of carrot?
choices: By conduction, from the outside in
quiz.explain: The center is the last part to heat.

quiz.q: Why do small pieces brown faster?
choices: More surface area for their size
quiz.explain: Browning happens on the surface.

quiz.q: Which cooking method needs the most even cuts?
quiz.explain: There are only minutes for heat to reach every piece.

sabbath.title: Gleaning: leaving the edges of the field (Leviticus 19:9–10; Ruth 2)
body: God's law built care for the poor into the harvest itself. "When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not reap your field right up to its edge, neither shall you gather the gleanings after your harvest. And you shall not strip your vineyard bare" (Leviticus 19:9–10). What was left was for the poor and the sojourner, the foreigner living among Israel. Deuteronomy adds the sheaf forgotten in the field, and the olives and grapes left on the branch, "for the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow," and gives the reason: "You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 24:19–22).

Ruth shows the law at work. She was a widow from Moab who came to Bethlehem with her mother-in-law, Naomi, at the start of the barley harvest. She went out to glean behind the reapers in the field of Boaz, a relative of Naomi's. Boaz told his workers to let her glean even among the sheaves and to pull out some stalks from the bundles on purpose for her (Ruth 2:15–16). By evening she had beaten out about an ephah of barley, perhaps 30 pounds (Ruth 2:17).

Gleaning fed the poor with dignity: they worked the harvest themselves, and the farmer gave by leaving, not by handing out. Gleaning groups still exist today, gathering crops left after a harvest for food banks.
steps: Read Leviticus 19:9–10 and Deuteronomy 24:19–22.
Read Ruth 2.
Answer in writing: who was gleaning meant for, and what reason does Deuteronomy give?
Answer in writing: what did Boaz do beyond what the law required?
With an adult, choose one way your family could "leave the edges" this week, such as cooking extra of this week's stir-fry for someone, or giving to a food bank. Write it down, and do it if you can.

quiz.q: In Leviticus 19:9–10, what were farmers told not to reap?
quiz.explain: The edges and the gleanings were left for the poor and the sojourner.

quiz.q: Whose field did Ruth glean in?
quiz.explain: Boaz was a relative of Naomi's (Ruth 2:1–3).

quiz.q: What reason does Deuteronomy 24 give for leaving the gleanings?
choices: Israel had been slaves in Egypt
quiz.explain: Deuteronomy 24:22.

weeks.note: A fine dice

drill.title: Timed dice: one onion, one pepper
body: Now you'll time yourself. Accuracy comes first: an even dice slowly beats a ragged one fast. Compare with your onions from week 9.
steps: Hone the knife and set up your board on a damp paper towel.
Start a timer and dice one onion into ¼-inch cubes. Stop the timer and write down the time.
Start the timer again and dice one bell pepper into ¼-inch cubes, skin side down. Write down the time.
Spread 10 cubes of each on the board next to a ruler. Count how many are within ⅛ inch of ¼ inch.
Write down your times and your count. Compare them with how the week 9 onions looked.
Use the onion and pepper in this week's Israeli salad, or store them for later in the week.

quiz.q: What matters more in this drill: speed or evenness?
quiz.explain: Speed comes with practice; uneven cubes cook unevenly.

quiz.q: Why cut the pepper skin side down?
choices: The blade doesn't skid on the skin
quiz.explain: The flesh side gives the knife something to bite.

knowledge.title: Name and size each classic cut
body: Cooks use names for each cut so a recipe can say exactly what it means. Sizes are a guide, not a law, but evenness always matters.

Large dice: ¾-inch cubes, for stews and roasting. Medium dice: ½-inch cubes, for soups and sautés. Small dice: ¼-inch cubes, for salsas and salads. Brunoise: ⅛-inch cubes, the finest dice, cut from a julienne.
Julienne: matchsticks ⅛ inch thick and 2 to 3 inches long. Batonnet: thicker sticks, ¼ inch thick and 2 to 3 inches long; cut across, they make a small dice.

Chiffonade: leafy herbs or greens stacked, rolled up tight, and sliced across into thin ribbons. Mince: chopped finer than a brunoise, with no set shape, like garlic or parsley. Chop: rough pieces, roughly the same size, when looks don't matter.

Notice how the cuts build on each other: planks become sticks (julienne or batonnet), and sticks become cubes (brunoise or small dice). This is the unit quiz: answer from memory, then review anything you missed in weeks 9 to 11.

quiz.q: What size is a small dice?
quiz.explain: ¾ inch is large; ⅛ inch is brunoise.

quiz.q: What is a brunoise cut from?
quiz.explain: ⅛-inch sticks cut across make ⅛-inch cubes.

quiz.q: What is a chiffonade?
choices: Leaves rolled tight and sliced into thin ribbons
quiz.explain: Used for basil, mint, and greens.

quiz.q: How thick is a batonnet?
quiz.explain: Cut across, it makes a small dice.

quiz.q: Unit review: in the claw, what guides the side of the blade?
quiz.explain: Fingertips stay curled back.

quiz.q: Unit review: what does honing do?
choices: Pushes the bent edge back into line
quiz.explain: Sharpening grinds a new edge.

quiz.q: Unit review: why must herbs be dry before mincing?
quiz.explain: Dry leaves cut clean.

quiz.q: Unit review: a piece twice as thick takes about how long to cook through?
quiz.explain: Time grows with the square of the thickness.

quiz.q: Unit review: which part of the knife is best for cutting a hard carrot?
quiz.explain: The heel is the strongest part of the edge.

sabbath.title: Prep and store a full set of salad vegetables
body: With an hour of knife work, you can have the makings of salads ready for several days. Many families prep a set like this so meals later in the week come together in minutes, or so they can focus on resting.
Greens: wash and dry them completely, then store them loosely in a container or bag lined with a paper towel. They keep 3 to 5 days.
Sturdy vegetables (carrots, peppers, radishes, red onion, celery) keep 3 to 5 days cut, each in its own lined container.

Tender ones (cucumbers and tomatoes) are cut the day you eat them; they turn soft and watery. Dressing keeps a week in a sealed jar in the fridge; shake it before using. Dress a salad only right before it's eaten.
steps: Wash and dry a head of lettuce or a bag of greens, and store it in a lined container.
Julienne or dice carrots and peppers, and slice a red onion thin. Store each in its own lined container.
Shake together a simple dressing in a jar: 3 parts olive oil to 1 part lemon juice or vinegar, with salt and pepper.
Label everything with the date.
Over the next few days, put a salad together from the containers, cutting cucumber and tomato fresh, and note how long it took.

quiz.q: Which salad vegetables are cut on the day you eat them?
quiz.explain: They go soft and watery when cut ahead.

quiz.q: When do you dress a salad?
quiz.explain: Salt in the dressing draws water out of the vegetables.

weeks.note: A sofrito base

recipes.title: Thick beef burgers
recipes.about: Thick, juicy beef burgers seared in a skillet and checked with a thermometer until they reach 160°F in the middle, on toasted buns.

recipes.title: Sandwich loaf
recipes.skill: Kneading to a windowpane, baking a loaf
recipes.about: A soft white sandwich loaf, kneaded until the dough stretches thin, proofed in a loaf pan, and baked to 190°F inside.

recipes.title: Dinner rolls
recipes.about: Soft, buttery pull-apart rolls, each weighed so they bake evenly, with two or three shaped as knots or small braids.

recipes.title: Tabbouleh
recipes.about: A bright parsley salad with mint, tomato, and a little bulgur, dressed with lemon and olive oil. The knife work is the dish.

recipes.title: Israeli salad
recipes.about: Cucumber, tomato, and pepper diced small and even, with parsley, lemon, and olive oil.

recipes.title: Garlic green beans
recipes.about: Green beans blanched bright green, then sautéed in shimmering oil with garlic until just blistered.

recipes.title: Beef picadillo
recipes.about: Ground beef browned over a sofrito of onion, pepper, and garlic, simmered with tomato, raisins, and olives, over rice.

recipes.title: Cajun rice dressing with beef
recipes.skill: An onion, celery, and pepper base, deglazing a pan
recipes.about: Louisiana rice dressing: ground beef browned with onion, celery, and bell pepper, the pan deglazed, and cooked rice stirred through.

recipes.title: Rice pilaf
recipes.about: Long-grain rice toasted in butter with a few broken noodles, then simmered in broth until every grain is separate.

recipes.title: Roasted vegetables
recipes.skill: Even cuts that roast at the same rate
recipes.about: A sheet pan of carrots, potatoes, peppers, and onion, cut so they roast evenly and brown at the edges.

recipes.title: Roast chicken pieces
recipes.about: Bone-in chicken thighs and breasts roasted with herbs until crisp, each checked with a thermometer: 165°F.

recipes.title: Baked fish with lemon and herbs
recipes.skill: Baking fish gently, checking pin bones
recipes.about: Salmon, cod, or tilapia fillets baked with lemon, dill, and garlic until they flake and reach 145°F, with a side timed to finish at the same time.

recipes.title: Steamed fish with ginger and scallion
recipes.about: White fish fillets steamed on a plate in a covered pot, then topped with ginger, green onion, soy, and a little warm oil.

recipes.title: Cod poached in tomato sauce
recipes.about: Cod fillets poached gently in a garlicky tomato sauce with olives and capers until they flake.

recipes.title: Pan-seared trout
recipes.about: Trout fillets seared skin-side down until the skin is crisp, finished with butter and lemon.

recipes.title: Vegetable stock
recipes.about: A clear stock from onion, carrot, celery, and herbs, simmered gently, skimmed, and strained, for soups later.

recipes.title: Chicken stock
recipes.about: The carcass from week 28's roast chicken, or chicken wings or backs, simmered slowly with vegetables, strained, cooled fast, and the fat lifted off.

recipes.title: Beef tacos with pico de gallo
recipes.skill: An even dice for pico de gallo
recipes.about: Seasoned ground beef browned to 160°F in warm tortillas, topped with a fresh pico de gallo of diced tomato, onion, jalapeño, and cilantro.

recipes.title: Kuku sabzi
recipes.skill: A big pile of finely chopped herbs
recipes.about: A Persian herb frittata: parsley, cilantro, dill, and green onion chopped fine, bound with eggs, and baked until set at 160°F.

recipes.title: Cuban black beans and rice
recipes.skill: Soaking and simmering dried black beans
recipes.about: Dried black beans soaked, simmered until creamy, and finished with a sofrito of onion, pepper, and garlic, over rice.

recipes.title: Bulgur pilaf with chickpeas
recipes.skill: Toasting bulgur, then cooking it by absorption
recipes.about: Coarse bulgur toasted in olive oil with onion and tomato paste, then simmered in broth with chickpeas until the liquid is gone.
